scope.basis: All 21 figures in the current project, plus three omitted named characters, a separately identified royal father, and key individually distinguishable unnamed figures.
scope.coverage_limit: Generic armies, crowds, most fleeting functionaries, family members mentioned only in passing, animals, illustrative parable figures, and names merely cited from other literature are not assigned invented individual cards. Further scope candidates are listed in the audit file.
scope.frame_policy: Rustaveli is retained from the project as an explicitly separate author/narrator card. Tamar, David, and other framing or literary names remain in the scope-review inventory rather than the fictional cast.
scope.confirmed_scope: Named cast and key unnamed figures

portrait_system.shared_style: Existing selected manuscript-inspired painted medallions with petrol-blue field and gold rim.
portrait_system.shared_framing: Centered circular artwork. The21 painted portraits use the same asset on their own front and every interaction thumbnail; the14 generic silhouettes appear only on their own fronts.
portrait_system.identity_rule: One stable visual identity per character. Apply the same portrait treatment across the deck once a direction is chosen.

card_contract.existing_assets: Selected painted PNGs and generated generic silhouette PNGs are artistic representations, not evidence of canonical appearance. Generic silhouettes do not establish an individual likeness.
card_contract.canonical_cues: Only appearances or scene-specific garments supported by the checked poem text. An empty array means no literal cue was established.
card_contract.narrative_motifs: Optional symbolic visual ideas derived from the story; these do not establish literal appearance or an approved design.
card_contract.review_stage: A5 full-deck proof with21 selected painted portraits and14 generated generic silhouettes on their own fronts. Relationships show painted portraits only; simplified chapter heading and no legend.
card_contract.size_intent: Moderately large cards that can comfortably be held in the hand.
card_contract.language_policy: Render one language on each physical card. Retain localized names in the data as references; this sample uses English only.

chapter_visualization.placement: back footer, replacing printed source-chapter citations
chapter_visualization.unknown_data_policy: All35 profiles have reviewed draft masks. The Sea King’s son has no depicted chapter appearance; Rustaveli marks explicit frame chapters1/65.
chapter_visualization.definition: Depicted scene participation, including flashbacks and direct narration or authored letters. Passing mentions, recipient-only references, and another character's brief recap of an absent person do not count.

ticks.alignment: chapter circle centers, including group spacing

interaction_visualization.coverage: Print only recorded contacts with a selected finished painted portrait. Exclude generic silhouettes even when their asset path resolves. Preserve the complete interacted_with data.
interaction_visualization.identity_rule: Use the same character portrait as that character’s own front; never substitute another character’s portrait.
interaction_visualization.missing_portrait: Retain a generic silhouette and portrait-pending label on that character's own front. Omit that character from relationship galleries until a painted portrait is selected.
interaction_visualization.empty_list: An empty array means no verified interaction within this carded cast. Narrator references do not become fictional encounters.
interaction_visualization.layout_note: Printed text remains compact; larger A5 typography and portrait-only contact galleries use the same sourced content.

episode_visualization.placement: back footer, replacing the 65-chapter presence strip
episode_visualization.definition: Active poem participation in the episode chapters OR explicit board token action (placement, movement, grouping, or removal) in token_action_ka.

editorial_policy.facts: Front descriptions, overviews, and key actions summarize checked narrative passages.
editorial_policy.insights: Every insight is explicitly marked interpretation, with its source chapters.
editorial_policy.unnamed_people: Descriptive labels identify roles; they are not invented personal names.
editorial_policy.minor_characters: Limited evidence is stated rather than filled with invented personality, biography, appearance, or fate.
editorial_policy.source_reference_system: Source ranges locate records in the local chapter JSON using stanza_number. They are not a claim that attached Georgian and English fields are aligned verse for verse.
editorial_policy.alignment_caution: The bilingual corpus contains offsets and late-chapter gaps or mismatches. Character notes identify checked Georgian passages where needed. Use chapter references for display until edition-specific verse citations receive a separate pass.
editorial_policy.visual_language: Poetic comparisons such as sun, ruby, crystal, or lion are not converted into literal eye colors, complexion, anatomy, or a fixed ethnicity.
editorial_policy.name_normalization: Display names use Fatman, Pridon, and Davar. Alternate project and translation spellings are kept as aliases.
editorial_policy.interactions: Source-supported encounters, actions, explicitly narrated care/custody, directed assistance, joint actions, or actual correspondence (including directed messages through intermediaries). Mere kinship, employment, shared crowd presence, mentions, and proposed marriages do not establish contact. Lists are reciprocal, omit self-links, and use stable profile IDs. Evidence and excluded/uncertain pairs are in the interaction catalog.

front.short_description: A searching knight whose devotion to Tinatin develops into sworn friendship with Tariel.

back.overview: Avtandil commands Arabia’s forces and loves Tinatin. Her request sends him after the mysterious knight, whose grief draws him into sworn friendship. Defying Rostevan’s refusal of leave, he searches for Nestan, secures vital information, and helps storm Kadjeti before returning to marry Tinatin.
key_actions: Finds Tariel, learns his history, and promises to return.
Leaves Arabia without permission to continue helping his sworn brother.
Finds Nestan’s trail and joins Tariel and Pridon at Kadjeti.

insights.text: His concern for Tariel expands a quest begun in romantic service into a demanding commitment to friendship.
His threats against Asmat and killing of Fatman’s lover complicate any reading of his resourcefulness as morally uncomplicated.

relationships.name: Tinatin
relationships.relationship: Beloved; later wife and fellow ruler
relationships.detail: Her commission begins his search; their exchanged promises sustain him during separation.

relationships.name: Tariel
relationships.detail: Learning Tariel’s suffering leads him to promise practical help and ultimately join the rescue of Nestan.

relationships.name: Asmat
relationships.detail: After coercion fails, he gains her confidence; she brings him to Tariel and later helps him find his distressed friend.

relationships.name: Shermadin
relationships.detail: He entrusts Shermadin with his frontier, forces, household, and messages during his absences.

canonical_cues: A young, initially beardless man, with a graceful form compared to a cypress.
His smile reveals shining white teeth.
At the opening hunt he wears crimson hunting apparel and a golden veil and rides a white horse.
Later in the search, dark facial hair is suggested by the jet-on-crystal metaphor.
narrative_motifs: A bow recalling the hunting contest and solitary journeys.
A letter recalling his testament and the search carried by messages.
A pearl token recalling his bond with Tinatin.

editorial_notes: The opening beardless description is explicit in Georgian stanza 40. Stanza 193 uses a jet-on-crystal facial metaphor; the local English makes the beard-growth interpretation explicit. A portrait must choose a narrative moment rather than combine incompatible ages.
Crimson apparel, golden veil, and white horse belong specifically to the opening hunt in stanza 72; they are not his permanent uniform.
Cypress, sun, crystal, and ruby are poetic comparisons. They do not establish a precise height, eye color, or literal gemstone-colored complexion.
The Asmat encounter includes seizing her hair and threatening her with a knife before he abandons coercion; it should not be retold as courtesy from the outset.
Fatman’s lover is the figure indexed by the project as chashnagiri; the killing and its guards should not be softened into a harmless disguise trick.

front.role: Commander of India; knight in the panther’s skin
front.short_description: Nestan’s lover, whose withdrawal into grief is interrupted by Avtandil’s friendship and their shared search.

back.overview: Tariel, Saridan’s son and India’s commander, loves Nestan-Darejan and kills the foreign prince selected to marry her. After Nestan is taken away, he searches unsuccessfully and withdraws with Asmat to the wilderness. Avtandil and Pridon help him rescue her from Kadjeti.
key_actions: Kills the proposed bridegroom, then defends his claim to India.
Tells Avtandil his history and accepts his help finding Nestan.
Leads one assault at Kadjeti and reunites with Nestan.

insights.text: His overwhelming grief complicates heroic strength: military prowess alone cannot restore the relationships on which his life depends.
The panther skin turns remembered love into a visible emblem, while friendship reconnects his private suffering with action.

relationships.name: Nestan-Darejan
relationships.detail: They pledge themselves to each other and plan the bridegroom’s killing.

relationships.name: Avtandil
relationships.detail: Avtandil searches for Nestan and joins Tariel in the rescue.

relationships.name: Pridon
relationships.detail: They exchange assistance and fight together at Kadjeti.

relationships.name: Asmat
relationships.detail: She carries the lovers’ messages and remains with him in exile.

canonical_cues: At his first appearance he wears a long garment with a panther-skin outer covering and panther-skin cap.
At the stream he holds a black horse by its rein and carries an exceptionally thick whip.
His bridle, armor, and saddle are adorned with pearls at that first encounter.
narrative_motifs: The panther skin recalls Nestan.
The cave shelters grief and later contains equipment for the rescue.

editorial_notes: The killing is intentional; the plan to spare the bridegroom’s army must not be rewritten as an entirely bloodless episode.
Tariel’s claim to India is an argument he voices, not an independently adjudicated modern legal finding.
Sun, lion, crystal, and rose comparisons are poetic language; they do not establish a literal complexion, ethnicity, or facial anatomy.

front.role: Princess and heir of India; Tariel’s beloved
front.short_description: A politically active lover whose choices, enforced separation, escape, and letters shape the poem’s central search.

back.overview: Nestan, Parsadan’s daughter and acknowledged heir, secretly pledges herself to Tariel. She urges his campaign against Khataeti and later directs him to kill the imposed bridegroom while sparing the army. Sent away by Davar, she endures captivity, escapes one court, and sends letters from Kadjeti.
key_actions: Declares her love for Tariel and urges action against Khataeti.
Directs the bridegroom’s killing while arguing against slaughtering his army.
Sends letters and a veil token from captivity in Kadjeti.

insights.text: Her letters make her an active participant in the search, even while imprisonment severely limits her physical freedom.
Her succession arguments and instructions about the bridegroom complicate any reading of her as merely a passive rescued princess.

relationships.name: Tariel
relationships.detail: She declares her choice and directs the plan against the bridegroom.

relationships.name: Asmat
relationships.detail: Asmat carries her messages and witnesses her removal.

relationships.name: Fatman
relationships.detail: Fatman shelters her and later reaches her through a messenger.

relationships.name: Parsadan
relationships.detail: His proposed marriage conflicts with her pledge to Tariel.

canonical_cues: She wears green clothing during the private meeting with Tariel in chapter 17.
During the dispute over her arranged marriage, she wears the veil Tariel gave her over the same green garment.
narrative_motifs: Letters preserve her voice across distance.
The veil changes from a love gift into a token sent from captivity.

editorial_notes: Her instruction is to kill the bridegroom while sparing his army; the profile neither omits her agency nor treats that instruction as nonviolent.
Her letter warns Tariel against dying in a rescue attempt; it is not a confident invitation to attack.
Green clothing is tied to particular scenes, not asserted as her only costume throughout the poem.

front.short_description: A crowned ruler whose generosity, love, and command set Avtandil’s search in motion.

back.overview: Tinatin becomes sovereign of Arabia while Rostevan is alive, immediately putting his lesson in generosity into practice. She sends Avtandil to find the mysterious knight, pledges her love to him, and later supports his promise to Tariel. She eventually marries Avtandil and forms a sworn sisterhood with Nestan.
key_actions: Distributes her accumulated treasure after receiving her father’s counsel.
Sends Avtandil to find the stranger and pledges her love.
Encourages Avtandil to honor his sworn promise to Tariel.

insights.text: Her command initiates the search, giving her a determining role in the adventure despite her remaining in Arabia.
By endorsing Avtandil’s return to Tariel, she allows devotion to a friend to coexist with their love.

relationships.name: Rostevan
relationships.detail: Her father crowns her during his lifetime and teaches her the royal value of generosity.

relationships.name: Avtandil
relationships.detail: She commissions his search, exchanges promises with him, and supports his obligation to Tariel.

relationships.name: Nestan-Darejan
relationships.detail: The two women meet in Arabia and part with the affection and oath of adopted sisters.

relationships.name: Shermadin
relationships.detail: He announces Avtandil’s return to her; she rewards him and his company.

canonical_cues: Long hair around a white neck; black eyelashes.
Dark hair is explicitly compared with jet in her later throne scene.
Wears a crown, holds a sceptre, and is clothed in royal garments at her coronation.
In the private audience she wears ermine and costly veils; a crimson veil is also specified.
At the homecoming she wears royal purple with her sceptre and crown.
narrative_motifs: An open treasury or scattered gifts recalling her first act of generosity.
A pearl love-token recalling her encouragement of Avtandil.

editorial_notes: Royal authority is explicit: she is enthroned while Rostevan lives. She should not be reduced to a waiting princess.

The physical cues are checked against Georgian stanza 123 (ermine, veils, eyelashes, long hair, white neck), 124 (crimson veil), 694 (jet-black hair), and 1540 (royal purple). Local English attachment differs by one stanza around the private audience.
Sun, rose, crystal, and ruby descriptions are poetic comparisons, not literal eye colors or a fixed skin palette.
No precise age, eye color, or historical costume cut is established by the checked passages.

front.short_description: A messenger and caretaker whose testimony and mediation connect the separated lovers with their helpers.

back.overview: Asmat carries messages between Nestan and Tariel and reports Nestan’s violent removal from India. She stays with Tariel in the wilderness, introduces Avtandil to him, and receives the news of Nestan’s survival. After their return, Tariel grants her one seventh of India.
key_actions: Carries the lovers’ messages and reports Nestan’s removal to Tariel.
Withstands Avtandil’s threats before arranging his meeting with Tariel.
Remains beside Tariel and later receives a share of India.

insights.text: Her care and mediation make sustained friendship possible, giving essential narrative weight to work outside the poem’s battles.
Her refusal to disclose Tariel’s history under threat presents trust as something that coercion cannot reliably produce.

relationships.name: Nestan-Darejan
relationships.detail: She carries Nestan’s messages and remains committed to finding her.

relationships.name: Tariel
relationships.detail: She tends him in the cave and is later rewarded with territory.

relationships.name: Avtandil
relationships.detail: Their first encounter is coercive; she later brings him to Tariel.

canonical_cues: She is described wearing black when Tariel returns to the cave in chapter 8.
narrative_motifs: Messages join separated people.
Water and tending accompany her care of the fainting Tariel.

editorial_notes: Chapter 64 Georgian stanzas 1649–1653 contain her territorial grant and marriage; the English translation is misaligned into earlier numbered entries.
The unnamed husband in chapter 64 is not given a personal name.
The phrase describing a black woman during Nestan’s assault has an uncertain referent; this profile does not use it to assign Asmat a complexion.

front.role: King of Mulghazanzar; sworn brother of the knights
front.short_description: A wounded ruler first helped by Tariel who later supplies information, guidance, troops, and hospitality to the companions.

back.overview: Pridon rules Mulghazanzar. Tariel encounters him wounded after an ambush by his cousins and helps him defeat them. Pridon shares his earlier sighting of Nestan, supports the later search, guides the allies to Kadjeti, and hosts Tariel and Nestan’s wedding.
key_actions: Shares his sighting of Nestan and sends sailors to seek her.
Guides the brothers toward Kadjeti with three hundred chosen horsemen.
Fights at one gate and later hosts Tariel and Nestan’s wedding.

insights.text: His alliance with Tariel begins in reciprocal aid, making friendship something enacted through healing, hospitality, information, and shared danger.
His practical knowledge of sea routes and Kadjeti complements the other knights’ courage, presenting cooperation as more than matching strength.

relationships.name: Tariel
relationships.detail: Tariel helps him against his cousins; Pridon helps search for Nestan.

relationships.name: Avtandil
relationships.detail: He helps Avtandil’s search and joins the expedition to Kadjeti.

relationships.name: Nestan-Darejan
relationships.detail: He once sees her at the coast and later joins her rescue.

canonical_cues: At his first encounter with Tariel he is wounded and holds a broken, bloodied sword.
He rides a black horse during that encounter, later giving the horse to Tariel.
narrative_motifs: A gifted horse joins the brothers’ separate journeys.
Sea routes connect his realm to the search and rescue.

editorial_notes: Pridon is the normalized English display name; Fridon and Wardrop’s P’hridon are aliases.
His cousins wound him in a dispute over an island; the checked account does not require saying that he had been deposed from his throne.
The wounds and broken sword belong to his first encounter, not every later appearance.

front.role: Gulansharo hostess and protector of Nestan
front.short_description: A merchant household leader whose shelter, gifts, and messengers reconnect the separated lovers.

back.overview: Fatman Khatun leads Gulansharo's merchant women and welcomes travelers into her household. She rescues and hides Nestan, supplies the jewels and horse that enable her escape, and later helps Avtandil recover her whereabouts. Her hospitality becomes a decisive source of shelter, intelligence, and communication.
key_actions: Shelters Nestan, then gives her jewels and a horse for escape.
Recognizes news of Nestan after overhearing a Kadji retainer's story.
Sends invisible messengers to Kadjeti and exchanges letters with Nestan.

insights.text: Her household connects private compassion with public networks of travelers, turning hospitality into an essential resource for the rescue.
Tariel's adoption of her as a sister recognizes protective care as a bond alongside the poem's sworn brotherhood.

relationships.name: Usen
relationships.detail: Entrusts him with Nestan's secret, then condemns his disclosure.

relationships.name: Nestan-Darejan
relationships.detail: Shelters her, enables escape, and sends letters to her captivity.

relationships.name: Avtandil
relationships.detail: First knows him as a merchant; later helps his declared rescue mission.

relationships.name: The Chashnagir
relationships.detail: His threats to expose Nestan's escape place her household in danger.

canonical_cues: Mature rather than young, lively, with a good figure, a full face, and a dark complexion (local stanza 1077).
Has an abundance of elegant gowns and head-dresses (local stanza 1077).
narrative_motifs: A garden window overlooking the harbor.
A letter, loose jewels, or a horse motif representing protection and escape.

editorial_notes: Her affair with Avtandil and her coercive former relationship with the Chashnagir are explicit; neither should erase her independent role in protecting Nestan.
Do not assign a specific gown color or jewelry design as canonical.

front.short_description: An aging ruler who crowns Tinatin and regards Avtandil as a foster-son.

back.overview: Rostevan, the aging ruler of Arabia, crowns his only child, Tinatin, and teaches her generosity. He loves Avtandil as a foster-son but resists his second departure to help Tariel. Their eventual reunion brings reconciliation, approval of the lovers’ marriage, and a renewed royal succession.
key_actions: Crowns Tinatin and counsels her to rule through generosity.
Refuses Avtandil’s request to leave Arabia and help Tariel.
Welcomes the returning friends and approves Avtandil’s marriage to Tinatin.

insights.text: The tension between paternal affection and royal command makes his resistance to Avtandil emotionally understandable without making it decisive.
His delight in Avtandil’s hunting victory suggests that mentorship can include welcoming the pupil’s superiority rather than resenting it.

relationships.name: Tinatin
relationships.relationship: Father and daughter; predecessor and successor
relationships.detail: He crowns his only child as sovereign and advises her to exercise mercy and generosity.

relationships.name: Avtandil
relationships.detail: He loves and trains Avtandil, opposes his second departure, and later welcomes him back and approves his marriage.

relationships.name: Tariel
relationships.relationship: Initially an unknown stranger; later an honored guest
relationships.detail: The pursuit of the grieving stranger ends violently; much later Tariel mediates the lovers’ marriage with Rostevan.

relationships.name: Sograt
relationships.detail: His trusted adviser can joke with him, but the request for Avtandil’s leave provokes severe royal anger.

canonical_cues: An aging man: he speaks explicitly of his old age.
Bearded: in grief he tears his beard.
narrative_motifs: A crown passed toward Tinatin, representing the opening succession.
A bow recalling his hunting contest with Avtandil.
An open hand recalling his counsel on generosity.

editorial_notes: Old age is explicit in chapter 2, especially stanzas 35–36 and 62. Beard-tearing is explicit in Georgian stanza 821; the associated English passage is attached to project stanza 820.
The epithet translated as exalted in stanza 32 should not be converted into an exact physical height.
Sograt’s identification with the later Arabian vizier is an editorial identification supported by the scholarship noted on Sograt’s card.

front.short_description: The confidant who keeps Avtandil’s household, forces, and secrets secure during his journeys.

back.overview: Shermadin is Avtandil’s trusted retainer, raised in close association with him and entrusted with his household, troops, and frontier while he travels. He keeps the first absence secret, brings news of his return, and later delivers Avtandil’s testament after the second, unauthorized departure.
key_actions: Administers Avtandil’s household and forces during his first long absence.
Carries news of Avtandil’s return to Rostevan and Tinatin.
Presents Avtandil’s testament to Rostevan after the secret second departure.

insights.text: Through him, the poem makes administration, secrecy, and dependable service essential to the more visible adventures of its heroes.
His request to accompany Avtandil shows that staying behind is an accepted duty rather than an absence of affection.

relationships.name: Avtandil
relationships.detail: Raised in close association with Avtandil, he receives authority over his household and forces while his lord travels.

relationships.name: Rostevan
relationships.detail: He reports Avtandil’s first return and later delivers the testament after the secret departure.

relationships.name: Tinatin
relationships.detail: He announces Avtandil’s return; she gives him and his company gifts.

narrative_motifs: A sealed letter recalling the authority and testament entrusted to him.
A frontier stronghold recalling the administration left in his care.

editorial_notes: The poem’s terms for his close upbringing and quasi-family loyalty do not establish that he is Avtandil’s biological brother or son.
No secure physical description was found in the checked passages. Hair color, eye color, beard, exact age, and uniform must remain artistic choices.
His service is an active administrative and communicative role; he should not be described as merely waiting for Avtandil.

front.role: Elderly vizier of the Arabian court
front.short_description: A trusted court adviser whose wit and intercession bring him close to royal affection and anger.

back.overview: Sograt is an elderly vizier close to Rostevan and a companion of Avtandil at court. He uses joking speech to ease the king’s melancholy. Later, he agrees to convey Avtandil’s request for leave despite fearing the king’s anger, and reports the knight’s secret departure.
key_actions: Jokes about Tinatin’s generosity to discover the cause of Rostevan’s sadness.
Carries Avtandil’s request for leave despite fearing Rostevan’s anger.
Returns to the king with news of Avtandil’s secret departure.

insights.text: His joking speech makes room for candor within a court where even trusted advisers must manage royal anger.
His reluctant intercession shows how friendship can expose an intermediary to dangers created by another person’s commitments.

relationships.name: Rostevan
relationships.detail: He can approach Rostevan with humorous counsel, yet the request for Avtandil’s leave exposes him to royal rage.

relationships.name: Avtandil
relationships.detail: They approach Rostevan together at the banquet; later the vizier advocates Avtandil’s request to help Tariel.

canonical_cues: Explicitly described as an old vizier at the coronation banquet.
narrative_motifs: A wine cup recalling his humorous approach to Rostevan.
A gesture of measured counsel recalling his role as intermediary.

editorial_notes: Sograt is explicitly named in chapter 2, stanzas 44 and 57–59. The later vizier is not reintroduced with that personal name in the checked poem text.
The local English renders stanza 737 as 'Vizier Ustasra'. NPLG’s Vepkhistqaosnis Lexicon defines უსტასრა there as palace chief or major vizier, a title rather than another person’s name.
Rustvelologia No. 5 identifies the later vizier’s statements at 742, 759, and 763 as Sograt’s words. The card follows that scholarly identification; no separate Ustasra character is created.

Lexical source: https://www.nplg.gov.ge/greenstone3/library/collection/lexikonebi/document/HASH478234338e86f1879190dc%3Bjsessionid%3D172A16E68CA1AFB0B8AD253C6738DC9E?ed=1 ; identification source: https://www.nplg.gov.ge/greenstone3/halftone-library/collection/period/document/HASH01cc60bb6f098c605e6fd037?ed=1 .
His explicit old age does not specify a white beard, baldness, eye color, or an exact costume. Those features must not be asserted as canonical.

front.short_description: Tariel’s foster father, whose marriage arrangement for Nestan precipitates a crisis within the Indian court.

back.overview: Parsadan rules six of India’s kingdoms before accepting Saridan’s allegiance. He and the queen raise Tariel and later have a daughter, Nestan. They arrange her marriage to a foreign prince. After Tariel kills him, Parsadan threatens Davar; he later dies before the lovers return.
key_actions: Receives Saridan into service and entrusts him with military command.
Raises Tariel and confirms him in Saridan’s office after mourning.
Arranges Nestan’s marriage and threatens Davar after the bridegroom’s killing.

insights.text: His paternal generosity and political authority become difficult to reconcile when his marriage arrangement conflicts with the lovers’ pledges.
The dispute reveals tension between choosing a successor through marriage and Tariel’s asserted claim through inherited royal status.

front.short_description: The self-named poetic voice who introduces the heroes and reflects on poetry and love.

back.overview: Rustaveli is the poem’s self-named poetic voice, introducing its heroes rather than joining their adventures. He praises Tamar, invites listeners to share Tariel’s sorrow, and reflects on poetry and faithful love. The closing verses reflect on time and place Rustaveli within a Georgian literary lineage.
key_actions: Names himself while presenting Tariel’s story in Georgian verse.
Praises Tamar and outlines his ideals of poetry and love.
Addresses listeners and reflects on the passing of human life.

insights.text: His invitation to mourn with Tariel encourages readers to approach heroic suffering through sympathy rather than distant admiration.
The discussions of poetry and love provide an ethical frame through which the later adventures can be interpreted.
